parts: Lesson 27: The Parrot Who Wouldn't Talk — Summary

This humorous story by Ruskin Bond is told by a ten-year-old boy. His Aunt Ruby buys a parrot (parakeet) and tries to teach it to talk, but the bird dislikes her and refuses. In the end it does learn to talk — repeating Aunt Ruby's own rude words back to her. The story shows that pets need proper care and kindness, and that rudeness comes back to us.

In those days almost everyone, Indian or European, kept a pet parrot or parakeet ('lovebird'). Some became great talkers or mimics, repeating mantras or advice such as 'Padho beta, padho!' or, for boys like the narrator, 'Don't be greedy!'. Aunt Ruby bought the parrot from a bird-catcher who sold caged birds door to door — budgerigars, munnias and even common sparrows dabbed with paint and passed off as exotic. Granny and Grandfather were not keen on caged birds, but Aunt Ruby threatened a tantrum, and her tantrums were 'dreadful to behold'.

The bird took an instant dislike to her and resisted all her sweet talk. When she cooed 'Kiss, kiss!', it backed away angrily, and once it lunged and knocked her spectacles off her nose. Then she became hostile, making faces and taunting it: 'You're no beauty! Can't talk, can't sing, can't dance!'

The narrator fed the parrot green chillies, ripe tomatoes and mango slices (eating a few mangoes himself). One afternoon, while everyone was having a siesta, he deliberately left the cage door open, and the bird flew to the mango orchard. He told Grandfather 'The door was quite loose.' Aunt Ruby was upset; they promised her goldfish — 'But goldfish don't talk!' — 'Well, neither did your bird,' said Grandfather, offering her a gramophone to listen to Clara Cluck instead.

A few days later the parrot, probably missing its green chillies, came back to the veranda railing; the boy unselfishly shared his mango. Aunt Ruby rushed out, crying that it had come back because it missed her. The parrot flew to a rose bush and shrieked in her own voice: 'You're no beauty! Can't talk, can't sing, can't dance!' Aunt Ruby went ruby-red and dashed indoors. It became a frequent visitor and said this every time it saw her. 'The parrot had learnt to talk after all!'

Kindness to animals and the love of freedom; caged birds suffer; we reap what we sow — Aunt Ruby's taunts came back to her. Humour comes from irony (the parrot learns exactly the words meant to insult it), the name pun ('went ruby-red') and the boy's gentle mischief.
